#10399. Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

We speak to Cognichip's Chief Product Officer, Stelios Diamantidis, about its new AI products

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Amid the AI gold rush, one particularly fruitful vein of research is the emergence of AI-assisted workflows in electronic design automation (EDA) tools like Cadence Maestro. One such company developing such foundational models is Cognichip, which in September launched Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), proprietary AI models developed specifically for semiconductor engineering. ACI deploys the 'industry’s largest training dataset' across semiconductor physics and chip design principles.

ACI Enterprise is Cognichip's deployable platform, which combines these specialized models with agentic workflows, project memory, and computing infrastructure for AI inference. The company describes ACI's approach as a self-learning flywheel, a continuously evolving design environment that brings together specifications, register-transfer level (RTL), and verification results to build a design that meets power, performance, and area (PPA) targets to Pareto limits. We sat down with Cognichip to learn more.

"We have surpassed, I think, over ten million training samples in our datasets that are either things that we designed ourselves directly or things that have been generated through our synthetic technology," says Stelios Diamantidis, Chief Product Officer at Cognichip, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "We have invented new ways of creating synthetic training samples for semiconductor design. And very importantly, now that we have all these data samples, characterized data samples, we also had to invent new models so that we can capture the data, and we also had to invent new pipelines for training so that we can map the training data to the models themselves."

Cognichip says ACI can analyze specifications, explore microarchitectural options, generate RTL, verify designs, identify and fix functional problems, and optimize designs to meet PPA targets. The system can also integrate existing IP modules and even produce FPGA implementations. In principle, ACI enables engineers to focus on product requirements and architectural decisions while ACI handles much of the logic implementation and verification work.

"Build the spec, build the RTL, estimate PPA, perform optimizations, run verification, everything," Diamantidis told us while explaining how ACI can develop and evaluate multiple architectural alternatives before engineers select the preferred design. "We do not try to turn the designer into a verification engine; our system is self-verified, so we want the designer to design, and we want our system not only to do the tasks but also verify them."

Because ACI operates as a self-learning flywheel, Cognichip claims engineers can revisit earlier architectural decisions and modify their designs without restarting the entire development process from scratch.

"Architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, all abstractions in the cognitive system are aligned, so the change in microarchitecture is essentially automatically reflected in RTL, and vice versa," Diamantidis explained. "Changes in RTL are automatically reflected in microarchitecture."

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Cognichip says it has participated in more than 40 customer engagements, including projects at Renesas and SiTime. According to the company, these engagements span a wide range of chip designs, from microcontrollers and encryption engines to networking processors, RISC-V CPUs, and AI accelerators.

To illustrate ACI's capabilities, Cognichip points to an evaluation conducted with an unnamed leading fabless semiconductor company. The customer provided an existing 55-page microarchitecture specification, which ACI used to explore architecture options, develop RTL from scratch, and integrate middleware and other components. The system also generated SystemVerilog testbenches, ran simulations, identified and corrected errors, and achieved functional verification closure with over 90% UVM coverage, the company claims. According to Cognichip, the entire process took just 10 days and required only one engineer. By contrast, doing the same job using conventional methods would require a full front-end design team and approximately 20 weeks, Cognichip says.However, there are several important caveats. First up, the customer had already provided a detailed 55-page microarchitecture specification, so the platform did not begin with a blank sheet. Secondly, Cognichip has not disclosed the complexity of the design, which makes it difficult to assess how much work has been done (or rather, processed). Finally, the reported acceleration applies to front-end engineering rather than the entire chip development process, which also includes physical implementation, tape-out, manufacturing, and silicon validation.

There is a substantial difference between developing functionally, conducting verified RTL, and prepping a chip design for manufacturing. Although Cognichip's ACI can develop microarchitectures, generate RTL, and optimize designs for PPA, the platform does not perform physical implementation. Tasks such as floorplanning, placement and routing, clock-tree synthesis, physical verification, and signoff still require conventional electronic design automation (EDA) tools from companies like Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens EDA.

"Today we do not do physical implementation," Diamantidis said. "So, place and route […] is done outside of our system."

This distinction matters because an architecture that meets its estimated PPA targets may fail to achieve them after physical implementation. For example, a design expected to operate at 1 GHz while consuming 15 W could achieve only 800 MHz at 20 W once engineers account for interconnect delays, clock distribution, buffering requirements, congestion, and other physical effects. Such discrepancies can require changes to RTL or even fundamental architectural elements, followed by another round of verification and physical implementation. In some cases, these iterations can consume weeks or months of engineering time.

"That cycle is very expensive in terms of time," Diamantidis said. "Because you are crossing design boundaries, and you are running very long runtimes and all that."

Cognichip claims that ACI can reduce these costly iterations by predicting the physical consequences of architectural decisions before implementation begins. According to Diamantidis, the company has trained its models on internally developed and characterized semiconductor designs, which enables ACI to estimate PPA characteristics and identify potential architectural trade-offs during front-end development.

"We have trained models with full physical stack visibility understanding so that the models can predict the PPA during the front-end design phase." "We can identify those trade-offs before going to physical implementation."

For example, ACI could recommend replacing two independent FIFOs with a single time-multiplexed FIFO to reduce power consumption at the expense of performance. Diamantidis used this hypothetical scenario to illustrate how the platform can evaluate architectural alternatives before engineers commit to a particular implementation.

"If you want to save power here at the cost of 10% of frequency, take these two FIFOs that you have for two different tasks, merge them, make one FIFO, and then time multiplex the two functions over one FIFO," Diamantidis explained.

Cognichip claims that ACI can estimate not only the immediate PPA consequences of such changes but also their potential impact on physical implementation.

"These trade-offs become visible now because we can tell the designer essentially in real time what some of these impacts are going to be to downstream parasitics and downstream congestion and all those kinds of effects."

The general idea behind ACI is to resolve potential architectural problems before RTL reaches physical design engineers rather than wait for implementation results and revise the architecture afterward.

"Our expectation is that there will be no loopbacks to the designer in terms of 'let us do this again because we did not meet this goal or because we ran into congestion issues,'" said Diamantidis.

However, the accuracy of these predictions is critical. Cognichip claims its models can predict certain PPA characteristics with errors of approximately 10% relative to results obtained from conventional EDA tools at the pre-route stage of physical implementation.

Cognichip evaluated its technology using 1,200 open-source designs and compared its predictions with those produced by general-purpose AI models, including Anthropic's Claude Opus and Google's Gemini. According to him, general-purpose models produced errors of approximately 50% – 100%, depending on the metric, whereas Cognichip's models reduced prediction errors to around 10%.

"[General purpose models] do not do well when it comes to predicting delays," Diamantidis said. "So, we take that down to within 10%. Again, 10% because think about it, we are running it at RTL. We do not have much physical information at all, right?"

There is an important distinction, though. Cognichip's reported accuracy refers to pre-route physical implementation results, not final post-route characteristics. Actual routing introduces interconnect and power delivery parasitics as well as other physical effects that can alter timing and power consumption. Consequently, the reported 10% prediction error does not necessarily mean that ACI-generated designs will achieve their estimated PPA targets after physical implementation and signoff.

Another question concerns the range of architectures and manufacturing technologies for which ACI can deliver such accuracy. Although Cognichip says its models incorporate semiconductor physics and account for process-dependent characteristics, it has not disclosed which foundry nodes it supports or how prediction accuracy varies across them.

Diamantidis explained that some architectural decisions are largely independent of manufacturing technology, whereas others become increasingly dependent on the target process node as development progresses.

"[Think about chip development as a tree], at the top of the tree, there are decisions that are not really foundry-specific; they are closer to microarchitecture," he explained. "Then, of course, as you start working your way down the tree, at some point you branch off because the decision may be targeted towards the TSMC node A versus TSMC node B, which will result in different prediction things. But there is a big trunk of decisions that are not really related to the node and are more related to the architecture and the way that the architecture is implemented. What we try to do is we try to think of this whole tree and provide a lot of feedback to designers, especially in a node-agnostic mode, and then, of course, at some point we have to become more node-aware."

This distinction is exceedingly important for complex CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators, where physical constraints tend to have substantial impact on architectural decisions. Meanwhile, Cognichip does not claim that ACI must develop such processors as monolithic designs. Instead, the company says its technology can work with individual IP blocks and subsystems, which engineers can subsequently integrate into larger chips. Of course, integration of these individually optimized IP blocks into larger chips is a challenge.

Although Cognichip says ACI can handle subsystems containing millions of logic gates (i.e., circuits that implement Boolean functions), combining multiple such designs into a complex SoC introduces additional constraints related to interconnect delays, clock distribution, shared memory bandwidth, power delivery, and floorplanning. Consequently, an architecture that achieves Pareto-optimal PPA characteristics as a standalone subsystem may no longer be optimal once integrated into a larger chip. According to Cognichip, ACI can account for these system-level interactions by aligning and optimizing individual blocks against global SoC and subsystem constraints.

“Yes, ACI can align and optimize individual blocks to global SoC and subsystem constraints. It can be applied to both flat and hierarchical optimization problems,” Diamanditis said.

Cognichip is not proposing a fundamentally new SoC development methodology, but rather automating substantial portions of conventional front-end workflows. Its ACI platform supports both flat and hierarchical optimization and can drive the partitioning and propagation of design constraints from the top level to individual blocks. According to Cognichip, ACI can decompose system-level constraints into requirements for individual components and then re-aggregate them as the blocks are integrated.

“ACI does not require a flat design methodology; it can drive hierarchical design from the top or subsystem-top down, ensuring that constraints are decomposed going into components but then re-aggregated when blocks are integrated,” Diamanditis explained.

According to Cognichip, ACI can handle individual IP blocks and subsystems containing millions of logic gates, which can subsequently be combined hierarchically into larger SoCs. The company emphasizes that the complexity of individual partitions, rather than their size, determines how effectively ACI can handle them. However, it remains to be seen how effectively ACI can coordinate architectural decisions and optimize PPA across an entire complex SoC in practice. After all, a Pareto-optimal CPU core, memory controller, and interconnect do not necessarily form a Pareto-optimal SoC, as their interactions introduce additional timing, bandwidth, power, and physical constraints.

Then again, developers of complex SoCs already address these challenges with hierarchical design methodologies, system-level optimization, and integration, so ACI’s focus on individual subsystems does not necessarily represent a significant limitation.

One of the questions that normally occurs when we talk about a tool that is only aimed at the front end of chip development is how it can handle feedback loops from physical implementation (more on this later). Such feedback loops occur when placement and routing reveal problems with timing, power consumption, die area, or routing congestion that cannot be resolved through physical design optimizations alone. In more serious cases, engineers must revise RTL, pipelines, memory hierarchies, or other architectural elements, which requires another round of functional verification, synthesis, and physical implementation. These iterations can take plenty of time and involve multiple engineering teams, which makes them particularly expensive.

Cognichip says ACI can use physical implementation results to revise RTL and microarchitecture if necessary, although this is not the company's primary focus. Instead, it aims to prevent costly iterations between front-end and back-end design teams by predicting potential problems before physical implementation begins.

"We are still focused very much on what we can do in the front end to prevent these situations rather than fix them."

If physical implementation reveals problems that require changes to RTL or microarchitecture, engineers can return to ACI with the relevant feedback (Cognichip does not specify with which file format that feedback must be submitted) and use the platform to revise their designs. Yet, ACI cannot resolve issues that require changes to the physical implementation itself, such as clock-tree synthesis or placement and routing.

"They can come back to our environments to provide additional guidance, additional prompting, additional information," Diamantidis said. "Then based on that information, we can of course perform an adaptation of the design […] if the issue can be addressed in the design itself, then of course we can do that."

Since feedback loops are expensive, yet necessary parts of semiconductor chip development flow, I had to ask that question explicitly, and the answer was that there would be no need for feedback loops with ACI. As the question and response require a lot of minutiae, we've added them in full below.

Anton Shilov: Can ACI ingest physical implementation reports from Cadence, Synopsys, or Siemens EDA tools, identify architectural bottlenecks, revise the microarchitecture, and RTL, and repeat the process until the design meets its PPA targets?

Stelios Diamantidis: Actually, this is where we depart from conventional approaches. We do not need to wait until physical implementation to identify these issues. We have trained models with full physical-stack visibility, which enables them to predict PPA during the front-end design phase.

For example, suppose you have one design that operates at a certain frequency and consumes a certain amount of power, and another that runs perhaps 20% slower but consumes significantly less power. We can identify these trade-offs before physical implementation.

Ultimately, the changes you want to make involve RTL and design constraints. Traditionally, engineers develop the RTL and constraints and hand them over to the physical implementation team. That team implements the design and reports the results. If the design fails to meet its targets, the front-end team must make changes, and the process starts again.

These iterations are very expensive in terms of time because they cross design boundaries and involve tools with long runtimes.

By training our models on the full physical stack, we can now provide immediate feedback to front-end designers. For example, we might tell an engineer: 'If you want to reduce power consumption at the cost of 10% of your frequency, take two FIFOs that serve different functions, combine them into one, and time-multiplex the two functions over that FIFO.'

That is just one example of a microarchitectural decision. We can make these trade-offs visible to designers in essentially real time because our models can predict their impact on downstream parasitics, routing congestion, and other physical characteristics.

As a result, engineers can make these decisions in a closed loop during front-end development. Once they have resolved the microarchitectural trade-offs and produced well-structured RTL, they can hand the design over to the physical implementation team. Of course, the design still has to go through physical implementation tools.

Our expectation is that there will be no need to return the design to the front-end team because it failed to meet its targets or encountered congestion problems. That is the fundamental change we aim to bring to the transition between front-end and back-end chip development.

Modern SoCs typically combine proprietary logic with third-party IP, including processor cores, memory controllers, interface IP, and other reusable components. However, developers do not necessarily have access to the RTL of licensed IP blocks, and licensing agreements may restrict how such information can be used. This raises the question of how ACI can integrate third-party IP without access to its internal implementation.

According to Cognichip, this is not a problem. ACI does not need to examine proprietary RTL to integrate an existing IP block into a larger design. Such IPs provide relevant interface specifications, including pin connections, signals, and their characteristics. ACI can then proceed with necessary integration logic and connect the IP to other subsystems.

"Most people want to take […] third-party licensed IP and optimize the integration of the IP," claims Diamantidis. "We ourselves do not ingest the guts of the IPs, nor do we try to train on any kind of data related to the IPs."

The CPO of Cognichip stressed that ACI Enterprise protects customers' IP within the company's firewalled data centers and prevents it from entering third-party AI training pipelines. The platform provides customer-controlled access to sensitive information, multi-tenant isolation, and security controls validated through a SOC 2 Type II examination. However, these protections do not supersede the licensing restrictions imposed by third-party IP providers.

Cognichip's ACI technology could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks such as architectural exploration, RTL development, verification, and PPA optimization.

The company's benchmark with a major chip designer suggests that the potential gains could be considerable, although the complexity of the project remains undisclosed. Such capabilities could be particularly valuable for startups and newcomers to the semiconductor industry, which tend to lack engineering resources and extensive IP portfolios of established chipmakers. By reducing the time, costs, and expertise required to develop custom silicon, ACI could lower the barriers to entry and enable smaller companies to pursue a custom silicon strategy that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive.

However, Cognichip has yet to demonstrate autonomous development of a complete, physically validated chip, let alone a sophisticated CPU or GPU. The company does not perform physical implementation, and its expectations of eliminating costly feedback loops depend on the accuracy of its PPA predictions. It also remains to be seen how effectively ACI can optimize complex SoCs that combine numerous proprietary and third-party IP blocks under common power, performance, and area constraints.

Ultimately, the Cognichip technology's value for leading-edge chip developers will depend not only on how quickly it can produce verified RTL, but also on how closely its predictions match the results of physical implementation and how much engineering work it can eliminate across the entire development cycle.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

#10398. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#10397. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

#10396. Architectural Choices in China's Open-Source AI Ecosystem: Building Beyond DeepSeek

This is the second blog in a three-part series on China's open source community's historical advancements since January 2025's "DeepSeek Moment." The first blog is available here, and the third blog is available here.

In this second piece we turn our focus from models to the architectural and hardware choices Chinese companies have made as openness becomes the norm.

For AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, architectural preferences, modality diversification, license permissiveness, small model popularity, and growing adoption of Chinese hardware point to leadership strategies across a multitude of paths. DeepSeek R1's own characteristics inspired overlap and competition, and contributed to heavier focus on domestic hardware in China.

In the past year, leading models from the Chinese community had almost unanimously moved toward Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including Kimi K2, MiniMax M2, and Qwen3. R1 itself was an MoE model, it also proved a crucial point: strong reasoning could be open, reproducible, and engineered in practice. Under China's real-world constraints, maintaining high capability while controlling cost, and ensuring models could be trained, deployed, and widely adopted, MoE emerged as a natural solution.

MoE is like a controllable compute distribution system; under a single capability framework, compute resources are allocated across requests and deployment environments by dynamically activating different numbers of experts according to task complexity and value. More importantly, it does not require every inference to consume the full set of resources, nor does it assume that all deployment environments share identical hardware conditions.

The overall direction of Chinese open-source models in 2025 was clear: not necessarily the strongest possible performance, but ability to operate sustainably, deploy flexibly, and evolve continuously, achieving the best cost performance balance.

Starting in February 2025, open-source activity was no longer focused only on text models. It quickly expanded into multimodal and agent-based directions: Any-to-Any models, text-to-image, image-to-video, text-to-video, TTS, 3D, and agents all progressed in parallel. What the community pushed forward was not just model weights, but a full set of engineering assets, including inference deployment, datasets and evaluation, toolchains, workflows, and edge-to-cloud coordination. The parallel emergence of video generation tools, 3D components, distillation datasets, and agent frameworks pointed to something larger than isolated breakthroughs---it pointed to reusable system-level capabilities.

The competition to lead similar to DeepSeek in a non-text modality heated up. StepFun's released high performance multimodal models, excelling in audio, video, and image generation and processing or editing. Their latest speech-to-speech model Step-Audio-R1.1 boasts state-of-the-art performance, beating proprietary models.  Tencent also reflected this shift through open-source work in video and 3D. Its Hunyuan Video models and projects such as Hunyuan 3D reflect growing competition beyond text-centric models.

Models in the 0.5B--30B range were easier to run locally, fine-tune, and integrate into business systems and agent workflows. For example: Among the Qwen series, Qwen 1.5-0.5B has the most derivative models. In environments with limited compute or strict compliance requirements, these models were far better suited for long-term operation. At the same time, leading players often used large MoE models in the 100B--700B range as capability ceilings or "teacher models," then distilled those capabilities down into many smaller models. This created a clear structure: a few very large models at the top, and many practical models underneath. The growing share of small models in monthly summaries reflected real usage needs in the community.

https://huggingface.co/spaces/cfahlgren1/hub-model-tree-stats

After R1, Apache 2.0 became close to the default choice for open models from the Chinese community. More permissive licenses lowered the friction around using, modifying, and deploying models in production, making it much easier for companies to move open models into real systems. Familiarity with standard licenses, such as Apache 2.0 and MIT, similarly eased usage; prescriptive and tailored licenses add friction through unfamiliarity and new legal barriers, contributing to the decline seen in the graph below.

Based on the releases of all organizations shown in Chinese Open Source Heatmap

In 2025, model releases increasingly aligned with inference frameworks, quantization formats, serving engines, and edge runtimes. A prominent goal was no longer just to make weights downloadable, but to ensure that models could run directly on target domestic hardware---and run reliably and efficiently. This change was most visible on the inference side. For example, With DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, both Huawei Ascend and Cambricon chips achieved day-zero support, not as cloud demos, but as reproducible inference pipelines released alongside the weights, enabling developers to validate real-world performance directly.

At the same time, training-side signals began to appear. Ant Group's Ling open models use optimized training on domestic AI chips to achieve near NVIDIA H800 performance, cutting the cost of training 1 trillion tokens by about 20%. Baidu's open Qianfan-VL models clearly documented that the model was trained on a cluster of more than 5,000 Baidu Kunlun P800 accelerators, their flagship AI chip, with details on parallelization and efficiency. At the beginning of 2026, Zhipu's GLM-Image and China Telecom's latest open model - TeleChat3, were both announced as being trained entirely on domestic chips. These disclosures showed that domestic computers were no longer limited to inference, but had started to enter key stages of the training pipeline.

On the serving and infrastructure side, engineering capabilities are being systematically open-sourced. Moonshot AI released its serving system: Mooncake, and explicitly supported features such as prefill/decoding separation. By open-sourcing production-grade experience, these efforts significantly raised the baseline for deployment and operations across the community, making it easier to run models reliably at scale. This direction was echoed across the ecosystem. Baidu's FastDeploy 2.0 emphasized extreme quantization and cluster-level optimization to reduce inference costs under tight compute budgets. Alibaba's Qwen ecosystem pursued full-stack integration, tightly aligning models, inference frameworks, quantization strategies, and cloud deployment workflows to minimize friction from development to production. Still, reports of compute constraints in China threaten expansion; Zhipu AI is reportedly restricting usage amid a computing crunch.

When models, tools, and engineering are delivered together, the ecosystem no longer grows by adding projects, but by structurally differentiating on a shared foundation-and beginning to evolve on its own. How China will respond to U.S. hardware sales and export controls as NVIDIA sells H200s continues to be an open question. Read more about the shifting global compute landscape here.

The "DeepSeek Moment" of January 2025 did more than trigger a wave of new open models. It forced a deeper reconsideration of how AI systems should be built when open source is no longer optional but foundational and why those underlying choices now carry strategic weight.

Chinese companies are no longer optimizing isolated models. Instead, they are pursuing distinct architectural paths aimed at building full ecosystems suited to an open-source world. In an increasingly commoditized model landscape, these decisions signal a clear shift in competition from model performance to system design.

Our next blog will go deeper into organizational wins and share some of what we expect to see in 2026.

Aggregated stats about derived models for an author.

This sentence is very insightful: In today's world where models are becoming increasingly homogeneous, these decisions mark a significant shift in the competitive landscape from model performance to system design. What China has made open-source has never been a single model weight, but the entire AI ecosystem.

I would love to hear your views on China's system design.

Really interesting anniversary post! It’s inspiring to see how the DeepSeek R1 release helped expand the global open-source AI ecosystem, lowering barriers and sparking new innovation over the past year.

Insightful analysis of architectural innovations in the open-source AI ecosystem! Understanding these different architectural approaches is crucial for making informed design decisions. When documenting our own system architectures and evaluating different approaches, I've found InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) incredibly valuable—it turns plain English system descriptions into architecture diagrams that you can iterate on through conversation. Makes it much easier to communicate architectural trade-offs and maintain living documentation.

One point that strikes me is that Chinese open source seems to have internalized something that the West still treats as secondary: when models become commodities, the real differentiator becomes systemic operability. It's not about "the best weight," but about who delivers a complete system—from training to inference—that works under real cost, hardware, and compliance constraints. This completely changes the axis of competition.

#10394. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

Even open-source isn't safe from Nintendo's legal team

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nintendo has set its famously litigious sights on the open-source firmware that powers hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch. Earlier this week, GitHub posted a DCMA request from Nintendo of America confirming that an entire network of 144 total repositories, including the parent repository, was taken down. Mod chip firmware for hardware including SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, and HWFLY was targeted.

Early original Nintendo Switch consoles shipped with an unpatchable hardware exploit found in the device's recovery mode, which has since been patched in later units such as the Switch Lite and Switch OLED (the modchip hack doesn't work on Switch 2). As such, running custom software on patched Switches requires hardware modification, soldering a microchip like a Picofly, HWFLY, or SX Core to your Switch's motherboard. These chips require firmware, specifically code that can perform the voltage glitching required during boot to hack the Switch.

Rather than playing whack-a-mole with vendors of off-the-shelf microcontrollers, Nintendo has instead issued a DCMA takedown notice to the entire family of GitHub repos hosting this firmware. "The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to mod chip firmware including but not limited to SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, or HWFLY," the DCMA request from Nintendo reads. "The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, during operation, the mod chip firmware at the reported repositories circumvents the technological protection measures put in place on the Nintendo Switch console by bypassing the boot sequence.

Nintendo went on to state that because these repositories are designed "primarily" to unlawfully circumvent technological measures controlling access to work protected under the DCMA, distributing mod chip firmware "constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is 'primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access' to copyrighted works." In support of this argument, Nintendo cited criminal proceedings brought by the US Department of Justice against Team-Xecuter, a maker and seller of SX Pro, SX Core, and SX Lite modchips.

While these modchips can be (and are) used for game piracy, they unlock a host of features including running homebrew and custom applications, emulation, alternative operating systems, and more. They also enable game modding, custom themes, and even Switch overclocking. Naturally, Nintendo has chosen to focus on their utility in accessing pirated games and bypassing DRM.

Because much of this hardware and firmware is already out in the wild, the move won't have any impact on existing Switch owners who have a modchip installed. However, this will prevent firmware updates to existing modchips, as well as firmware flashing and reflashing. Naturally, it will also prevent future potential hardware modders from hacking their Switch in the same way.

Nintendo is famous for its fervent prosecution of copyright law, but developments in AI are turning this into a drastically more complicated battle. Nintendo's Zelda remake was dumped online on the same day it launched on Switch 2, while earlier this year one developer used AI to bring the original Nintendo 64 version to iOS. In July, Mario Kart Wii was recompiled for PC in 4K with over 200 tracks.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10390. We Got Claude to Build CUDA Kernels and teach open models!

The best thing about agent skills is upskilling your agents on hard problems. There are two ways to look at that:

This blog post walks through the process of using a new tool, upskill, to generate and evaluate agent skills with large models and use them with smaller models. We will benchmark upskill on the task of writing CUDA kernels for diffusers models, but the process is generally useful for cutting costs, or using smaller models on hard and domain-specific problems.

In case you missed it, agent skills are taking the coding agent game by storm. In fact, they’re a straightforward concept to define model context as files, like instructions as markdown and code as scripts. The file format makes them easy to generate, share, and review. In short, they’re a practical medium to share capabilities across models and tools, and they're most useful in specific domains or hard problems. Not stuff the model can do well anyway.

This post showcases this process by using Claude to generate a Skill file that can be used by open source models for a complex and specialized task: write CUDA kernels. We first tried a simple skill based on existing documentation, and we found that it improved performance for some others, but not all. In fact, it could even degrade performance or increase token usage for some models. Check out the plot below to see the performance of the model with and without the basic skill.

Now, let's walk through how you can use upskill to upskill your agents on hard problems, and measure performance.

First, we use Claude Code to build a kernel interactively and export the trace. We worked through the process by instructing, validating, and adding documentation links. This somewhat naive process is important to reveal the models' initial challenges. In fact, you can iterate on this multiple times, by trying to solve the task with draft versions of the skill, and experimenting with smaller models. Each time, you can instruct the agent to improve the skill and test it on the smaller model.

Here's an example of the skill that we created and have been using to build kernels. We started from this agent trace where the agent was able to build a kernel, but not without some help.

Once the teacher model has performed the task, we need them to make a skill. There are a number of effective ways to do this.

In most cases, the first 2 options result in functional skills. However, the performance of an agent with the skill is unknown. That’s where upskill is useful, because it will also generate test cases for your skill based on the trace. It then compares the results under both scenarios: using the trace, or applying the skill. We see below that the original model (Claude Opus) met the same performance with and without the skill. This means the skill captured the task for this model. Great!

Finally, we need to transfer our newly created skill to the tool or model we intend to use. Most tools like codex, cursor, and opencode have settled on a consistent format for skills, which is a directory at {agent}/skills/{skill_name}/SKILL.md , so we just need to copy the skill directory to this location.

With upskill we can pass a skill and a set of models to the eval command and upskill will run the test cases on those models with and without the skill to compare performance. We can see here that the skill increases accuracy on some open models, but not on all.

In this case, we might want to iterate further on the gpt-oss skills by regenerating the skill. We can do upskill generate --from {skill}.

There is more to agent skills than model performance. Often agents can reach a given accuracy with or without a skill, they just need to consume more tokens to get there. For recurring tasks, we want to optimize agents to use less tokens to achieve the same accuracy. The results below reveal another dimension to the skill. Some models are significantly reducing their performance token usage, whilst others are using more tokens with the skill. For example, with moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Thinking the skill is clearly effective in terms of accuracy and token usage. However, for Claude Opus 4.5 there is no clear performance increase and an increase in token usage, so you would not want to use this skill with Claude Opus 4.5.

tldr; try out and evaluate models with the skills you create. Use upskill eval or a similar tool to evaluate the models performance with and without skills.

That’s the high level end to end of upskilling your coding agents on hard problems. Try out upskill now like this:

We have a high level understanding of how we can upskill an agent. Let’s now look at the use case we solved for writing CUDA kernels.

We didn’t just want to write kernel code, but understand the full kernel-builder workflow: project structure, build.toml configuration, architecture-specific optimizations, and PyTorch bindings. This tutorial shows how upskill creates validated skills that actually work.

The kernel-builder-cuda-kernels skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about CUDA development: which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:

And Claude will create the complete project structure, CUDA implementation, and build configuration—following the exact conventions that kernel-builder expects.

This isn't about generating boilerplate. The skill encodes domain expertise: H100 uses compute capability 9.0, shared memory should be aligned to 128 bytes, async memory copies require __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900. Knowledge that would take hours to gather from documentation gets packaged into ~500 tokens that load on demand.

That's it. Upskill uses Anthropic Claude Opus-4.5 model by default but also supports OpenAI and local models via OpenAI-compatible endpoints as generators. We want to use the more expensive and higher quality models to generate skills, and the smaller ones to use them. Think robin hood.

Let's walk through generating a skill that teaches agents how to build CUDA kernels with HuggingFace's kernels library.

Above we used upskill, but it could in fact be any agent or chat tool and an exported trace.

Also, we could start from an existing skill and add to it:

upskill loads the existing skill, applies your improvements, and re-evaluates to ensure the changes help.

upskill creates a skill, generates test cases, evaluates performance, and refines based on failures:

The baseline shows how the model performs without any skill. The "with skill" result shows performance after the skill is injected into context. A 35% improvement means the skill is working.

The skill is saved as a directory following the Agent Skills specification:

The important test is: does this skill help local or cheaper models to build kernels?

A 45% improvement on "unsloth/GLM-4.7-Flash-GGUF:Q4_0" means the skill successfully transfers domain knowledge from a capable model to a faster, cheaper one. Skills that work on weaker models will definitely work on stronger ones.

This is the core value proposition: use expensive models to create skills, then deploy those skills with cheap or local models.

upskill uses a teacher-student approach to evaluate models where the teacher model generates test cases for the student model to be evaluated on.

If you pass an existing skill to upskill eval, it will generate test cases for the skill and evaluate the model on them. Test cases are simple input/output pairs that verify the agent understands the task:

We can also test how a skill performs across different models:

This helps you find the cost-performance sweet spot: maybe Haiku with the skill is good enough for your use case, saving significant API costs.

We've shown that upskill can create validated skills that transfer domain expertise from powerful models to cheaper ones. The kernel-builder skill is just one example of what's possible.

The approach works for any specialized task where you'd otherwise write detailed prompts repeatedly. Skills are portable across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other tools that support the Agent Skills specification.
