#10359. Democrats announce a new effort to shape the AI agenda ahead of the 2028 presidential election

A Democratic political organization is announcing a new effort to shape how to talk with voters about artificial intelligence, deepening its investment on an issue that an increasing number of party leaders believe creates a stark contrast with President Donald Trump’s opposition to regulating the powerful technology.

Tomorrow Together was one of several groups that tried to counter the industry’s huge campaign war chest during the midterms. It pushed for new limits on artificial intelligence and data centers and spent $6.5 million on behalf of candidates calling for more regulation.

The latest research initiative, pegged at $1.1 million to start, begins as Democrats meet in Denver for the What’s Next conference, a two-day opportunity to celebrate their sweeping wins in midterm races and chart a course toward the next presidential campaign. It also comes after fresh warnings that the technology poses risks to humans as companies begin a new phase of development that will allow AI to build new versions of itself.

“We expect getting this right is going to be critical to winning people’s votes,” said Maddie Kriger, the group’s chief program officer. “It’s also not out of the realm of possibility we will see more and worse AI incidents in the next year, and we want to be prepared to move to help people and take action if that does happen.”

Democrats believe Trump has embraced a wildly unpopular position and handed them an opportunity to become the party that pushes for guardrails on AI development.

“I really think we’re watching the birth of a new political issue before our eyes,” David Shor, a prominent party data analyst, told the Denver crowd as he described AI as the rare issue where voters of both parties embrace regulation.

Karthik Ganapathy, a co-founder of Tomorrow Together, agreed.

“I’d rather be us than them,” he said of Republicans on the issue.

Some Republicans have distanced themselves from Trump’s pro-industry stance, most notably Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is widely believed to be preparing another run for the presidency.

Rob Flaherty, the other co-founder of Tomorrow Together, expects his party to still have the edge.

“At the beginning of the cycle, this was a jump ball. Voters didn’t know who to trust,” he said. Now, thanks to Trump, he argued, Democrats have the lead. “Regulating technology is where the voters are.”

This story has been corrected to show the name of the Democratic organization is Tomorrow Together, not Together Tomorrow.

—Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press

#10358. OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

OpenEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

OpenEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?"

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

To ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across users and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

Multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

Correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

For a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

In practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring issues.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

The agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

We can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

A new PETG ESD filament just entered the market, and it's a better value than the competition.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prusa released its new Prusament PETG ESD on Tuesday: a carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube (CNT)- filled, electrostatic-dissipative (ESD) PETG filament meant to protect static-sensitive electronics. While it’s great for enclosures for a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, and the like, Prusa is targeting the filament more toward electronics production than hobbyist use; however, it’s cheaper than the non-ESD Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber at only $56.99.

Prusa isn’t the only one selling ESD filament; 3DXTech and Polymaker were first to the scene, but Prusa is the first to include carbon fiber alongside carbon nanotubes to provide the ESD properties, improving dimensional accuracy and minimizing warping. 3DXTech sells its ESD-PETG at $105; Polymaker’s Fiberon PETG-ESD is $65.98, but the Prusament PETG ESD is only $56.99 and is the only one with carbon fiber reinforcement.

Non-ESD filaments are generally safe for electronics enclosures; many hobbyists use regular PLA, PETG, and ABS without any problems. And while the extra protection can be appreciated, Prusa positions this not for hobbyists, but for electronics production — PCB fixtures and holders for soldering, IC trays for handling and transport, holders for testing multiple boards at once, etc., as Prusa shows on the PETG ESD product page. It saves on manufacturing costs, reducing the need for CNC-machined ESD trays and fixtures, and can be quickly printed on-site with very little lead time. It’s not necessarily for big businesses only either, as indie hardware developers and smaller-scale manufacturers could use this filament to improve their production line without buying expensive ESD filament.

Prusa has not yet published the datasheet containing details about the strength of the filament, but Prusa claims that the filament has increased stiffness and reduced toughness, similar to Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber’s properties. However, the amount of carbon fiber in PETG ESD may be different from PETG Carbon Fiber, as the latter’s purpose is more for strength than for electronics manufacturing.

Prusa is known to use its own 3D printers to print its own components and use its own products for the 3D printers it sells, and on the product page, Prusa says it uses PETG ESD in its own production line to prevent overcoating the edges when powder coating its print sheets. While it isn’t the first or only ESD filament on the market, it’s certainly the cheapest, and when its strength profile is released or tested independently, it may potentially be more worth it than Prusa’s own PETG Carbon Fiber in certain cases.

#10356. High airfares could become the new normal, according to this industry insider

High airfares could become the new norm as airlines contend with soaring jet fuel prices and mounting operating costs, the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines’ chief said Friday.

Wong Hong, director-general of the association grouping 18 airlines in the region, said carriers were trying to contain ticket prices while protecting their finances and avoiding fare increases that could drive passengers away.

But the industry is operating in a substantially different cost environment from a year ago when jet fuel was about $80 a barrel, compared with around $180 currently, he said. Fuel accounts for a third of airline operating costs, making further price increases a threat to carriers’ financial performance, he said.

“I believe so,” Wong said after an AAPA conference when asked whether high airfares would become a lasting feature rather than a temporary adjustment. “We are living in completely different market conditions and a completely different cost environment … and it looks like these high prices will continue to prevail.”

On whether airlines could implement another round of fare increases if fuel prices remain high, Wong said there was no clear answer as passenger price sensitivity varies across markets.

Major airlines across the Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America have raised base fares, hiked fuel surcharges or added extra fees since the Iran war began in late February.

The AAPA’s data showed that passenger traffic across Asia-Pacific slumped for five consecutive months from April to August, before rebounding marginally in September. For the first nine months this year, overall passenger traffic in the region still grew by 1.9%.

“Airlines will try their best to hold on to the fares that they can charge without trying to lose passengers, but it is a tricky dilemma,” Wong said.

Airlines face a mismatch between ticket sales and fuel purchases, complicating their ability to manage rising costs, he said. Passengers often book flights months in advance, locking in fares before airlines purchase the fuel needed to operate those flights.

Beyond fuel costs, Wong said airlines continued to face supply side challenges including aircraft delivery delays and the high cost of maintaining older aircraft. But he said carriers had shown resilience and travel demand remained strong.

Airlines are doing their best to find the right levels in different markets to strike a balance between absorbing higher costs and pricing passengers out of the market, he added.

—Associated Press

#10355. Custom Kernels for All from Codex and Claude

tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

Writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

We gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:

This is domain knowledge that gets lost in documentation tabs and Stack Overflow answers. An agent skill packages it into context that loads on demand.

First, let's show how to use the skill right away, then we'll dive into the details of how we benchmarked the kernels.

The skill ships with the kernels library. Install it into your coding agent with a single command:

This drops the skill into .claude/skills/cuda-kernels/ where Claude Code and Cursor pick it up automatically. For other agents:

Or, you can go for something more open-ended:

The agent can read the skill, select the right architecture parameters, generate the CUDA source, write the PyTorch bindings, set up build.toml, and create a benchmark script.

If you're working on more complex kernels, or architecture-specific optimizations, that aren't covered in the skill, then the skill supplies the fundamental building blocks and patterns to get you started. We are also open to contributions on the skill itself.

The skill is roughly 550 tokens of structured guidance plus reference scripts, GPU optimization guides, troubleshooting docs, and complete working examples. Agentic coding tools like Codex and Claude can read this and produce a working kernel project.

When an agent loads this, it gets everything it needs to go from "write me an RMSNorm kernel" to a buildable, benchmarkable project. It will grep and glob the skill to find the relevant files and directories. So it's important to structure the skill in a way that is easy to find.

The agent is instructed to generate kernels that conform to the templates in references/kernel-templates.md and produce a complete kernel project:

The agent built RMSNorm, RoPE 3D, GEGLU, and AdaLN kernels for LTX-Video, a video generation pipeline from diffusers. The full example is at examples/ltx_video/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to check out the generated kernel, got to this example

First, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline. This is the main speedup in the optimized pipeline.

Average speedup: 1.88x and a bandwidth efficiency: 34.7% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Next, we compare the end-to-end video generation performance of the optimized kernels against the baseline (no compile) and the torch.compile baseline.

RMSNorm accounts for ~5% of total compute in LTX-Video. The remaining time is spent in attention, linear projections, and VAE decode. The 6% end-to-end speedup from a single kernel type is consistent with that profile.

The agent built an RMSNorm kernel for Qwen3-8B, a large language model from transformers with 65 RMSNorm modules across 32 layers. The full example is at examples/qwen3_8b/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to explore the kernel, check it out here.

Once again, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline.

Average speedup: 1.94x and a bandwidth efficiency: 22.3% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

The agent gives you a working kernel. The Kernel Hub lets you share it so anyone can load it without compilation. Here is the full path from agent output to published kernel.

The agent produces a project that already follows the kernel-builder layout:

The build.toml tells kernel-builder what to build. The agent generates this for you, including the correct cuda-capabilities for your target GPU:

Kernel Hub kernels must support all recent PyTorch and CUDA configurations. The kernel-builder Nix flake handles this automatically. Copy the example flake.nix into your project and run:

This builds the kernel for every required PyTorch/CUDA variant and places the results in build/. For faster builds, enable the HuggingFace Nix cache:

Create a model repo on the Hub and upload the built kernel:

Once published, anyone can use your kernel with zero compilation:

get_kernel detects the user's Python, PyTorch, and CUDA versions and downloads the matching pre-compiled binary. No builds, no flags, typically ready in seconds.

The skill and the Hub are complementary. The skill handles development. The Hub handles distribution. Build a kernel with the skill, validate it with the benchmark scripts, publish it to the Hub, and it becomes a one-liner for everyone else.

We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end. We benchmarked the kernels and found that the optimized kernels can provide a speedup in both isolated and end-to-end performance.

Installation with pip install kernels works, but the command has no skills option:

The kernels repo has kernels-builder and the kernels library.

This is the reason why doing a pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/kernels.git would not work.

Question: Is the baseline in section Isolated RMSNorm benchmark (Pytorch baseline) using torch.compile() or not? Custom kernels should be ideally beating torch.compiled code.

#10352. 7 E-commerce UX Tips for Selling Car Accessories and Home & Kitchen Products Online

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

A phone mount on a white background says nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

Mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

If your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

What are the most important e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

How should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

How big should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

How can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

Good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.

Venice-X maxes out the family's frequency for the first time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD missed out on deploying Turin-X CPUs in the previous generation, giving its 3D V-Cache tech a four-year hiatus from the data center following the launch of Genoa-X in 2023. In the second half of next year, 3D V-Cache is coming back for HPC with Venice-X, matching the 96 cores and 1,152 MB of L3 cache available on the EPYC 9684X (Genoa-X), but with vastly higher clock speeds, PCIe 6.0, and nearly four times the per-socket memory bandwidth.

After first bringing hybrid bonding to EPYC processors with Milan-X in 2022, AMD followed up a little over a year later with Genoa-X. Turin came and went without a chip sporting stacked SRAM, but now, it’s back with Venice-X. The critical change this time around doesn’t come from big jumps in core count — and consequently cache — as is the case with the standard SP7 lineup. Rather, it’s the 5.3 GHz boost clock speed, another pillar of Venice broadly, that’s particularly beneficial in the HPC workloads Venice-X targets.

As you can see from the top EPYC -X chips from previous generations, boost clocks were significantly lower for the X chips, and higher frequencies were available within the standard chips from each family. Milan scaled up to 4.1 GHz, while Genoa could climb to 4.4 GHz, just not on the EPYC -X chips. Venice-X brings up to the maximum 5.3 GHz boost clock available across the range, unifying a high frequency with a large pool of bonded L3 for HPC workloads.

There are still details missing about Venice-X, including the base frequency, how many SKUs are in the lineup and what their specs are, and the TDP (though the 400 to 600 W range available to other Venice CPUs is likely). The chips appear to use the SP7 socket, however, keeping with previous EPYC -X chips.

The platform comes with 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes, while the smaller SP8 platform targeting enterprises trades memory channels for PCIe lanes. Venice-X comes with the full 16-channel memory setup available on SP7, including support for MRDIMMs at 12,800 MT/s that can drive the quoted 1.6 TB/s of per-socket memory bandwidth.

The critical marriage with Venice-X for HPC workloads, according to AMD, is high frequency with a large pool of stacked cache. AMD currently maintains both 3D V-Cache and high-frequency EPYC chips in its HPC fleet to run its internal EDA workloads. AMD Fellow Phil Steinke says the company runs performance analysis on these workloads to characterize performance, optimize EPYC designs, and push partners to optimize their software.

The biggest consumer on the HPC fleet by far are function verification workloads at over half of AMD's used compute, according to Steinke. These are logic simulations that show up in tools like Cadence Xcelium, and Steinke says the EPYC team is running these workloads “24 x 7 x 365.”

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

An example of one such workload is above, measuring IPC with AMD's uProf monitoring utility. With 3D V-Cache, AMD says this workload completes 40% faster at around double the instructions per clock. AMD didn't clarify which chips it was comparing or what application it was using. However, the comparison is between an EPYC fleet with and without 3D V-Cache.

Steinke says AMD is able to now move toward a single chip with Venice-X, maintaining the cache advantages in workloads like functional verification while driving the EDA workloads more sensitive to frequency. "I mentioned we have a mix of high frequency and 3D V-Cache CPUs in our data center, and that's because through Milan and Genoa, the high frequency parts were always a little higher on the frequency side," Steinke said. "You don't have that dichotomy [with Venice-X]. You can get the best of both worlds in a single CPU, and this is what we're really excited to be picking up for our own use."

AMD hasn't shared any benchmarks for Venice-X yet, but it provided some more specific HPC benchmarks comparing its high-frequency EPYC 9686F to Intel's Xeon 6980P in several HPC workloads, such as computational fluid dynamics. In AMD's testing, the 9686F was 1.6x faster in these benchmarks while running 32 fewer cores.

We had a chance to test the EPYC 9686F along with the dense EPYC 9996, which you can read more about in our Zen 6 EPYC Venice deep dive and benchmarking article. And indeed, the EPYC 9686F looks very impressive in some of the HPC workloads we ran.

We were only able to test a 2P configuration, and as evidenced by the sole Xeon 6980P, CloverLeaf is sensitive to latency. Even then, the 2P EPYC 9686F completed the complex hydrodynamics simulation in about a third of the time as a single Xeon 6980P.

AMD says it's currently using MEXT, its AI-driven flash-as-DRAM technology, to bolster the amount of memory available for its EDA workloads. When it deploys Venice-X, Steinke says the company will continue using MEXT, which you can read more about in our recent MEXT breakdown on Tom's Hardware Premium.

Venice-X CPUs are launching in the second half of 2027, while SP7 and SP8 Venice CPUs are rolling out now. Also coming in the second half of next year is AMD's Verano, which it's pitching as an AI host node that leverages SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory.

#10349. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

#10348. Your burnout may be a boundaries issue

Below, Nabeela Elsayed shares five key insights from her new book, Breaking Burnout: How High Achievers Break the Success Myths Driving Exhaustion, Overwork, and Burnout.

Nabeela is a recovering workaholic and former C-suite executive. She began her career as a barista making $6.50 an hour and spent the next 20-plus years climbing the corporate ladder until she ran operations and people at companies including Walmart Canada and IKEA.

What’s the Big Idea?

Burnout isn’t a stamina problem. It isn’t a boundaries problem. It’s what happens when the definition of success you were handed was never survivable in the first place. Getting off the burnout loop isn’t a dramatic leap. It’s a series of small choices toward a life that no longer costs you yourself.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Nabeela herself—in the Next Big Idea App, or buy the book.

1. Fix your relationship with work, not just your job.

When I lived in Sweden, I learned about lördagsgodis—Saturday candy. Kids and grown-ups skip sweets all week and enjoy them on Saturdays. This is a country with a pastry shop on every corner, yet an entire society says “not today” six out of seven days. That’s not willpower. Back in the 1940s and 1950s, dental researchers discovered that how often you eat sugar does more damage than how much. Health authorities said: if you’re going to have it, have it once a week. That became a ritual in families.

Sugar is not a villain, and neither is work itself. We need to work, but like food, it can nourish or poison you depending on how often and how intensely you consume it. Most of us assume the problem is the job—the toxic boss or impossible workload—and sometimes it is, but usually it is a toxic relationship with work itself.

You can be in a great company with a great boss, or even be the boss, and have an unhealthy relationship with work. Chris Raney built the world’s largest HR podcast platform. He owns the company. No one’s forcing him to do anything. And one morning he got up, did his workout, took a shower, and tried to head to work, but he couldn’t move. He was having a major anxiety attack, frozen at the threshold of his front door. When I talked to him about it, he said, “It’s self-inflicted. It’s all self-inflicted.”

Changing jobs rarely fixes burnout because you bring your relationship with work with you. So before you update your resume, ask yourself: how healthy is your relationship with work?

2. Ask whether rest restores you.

The sports world has figured out something the rest of us haven’t. Athletes don’t wait for an injury to find out that they’ve been overloaded. Lauren Bushman, director of sports science for Canada Basketball, and her team work backward from the moments that matter—the playoffs or Olympics—and build capacity slowly over years. Recovery isn’t a reward. It’s part of the training plan. As Lauren told me, “You never mess with a basketball player’s pre-game nap.” And her measure of success is beautifully simple: Are her players healthy and ready when it counts?

“Recovery isn’t a reward. It’s part of the training plan.”

Now, think about how most of us work. We run an endless marathon at sprint speed. Nobody’s tracking our load, and we’re usually the last to notice something’s off. But a simple question can improve self-awareness; ask yourself: Does rest restore you? Exhaustion is running out of gas. You can refill the tank with sleep or a weekend off or a real vacation, and your energy comes back. But burnout is the engine breaking down completely. You rest, and nothing changes. The cynicism is still there, the detachment is still there, and the joy doesn’t come back.

Horacio Barbeito, my former CEO at Walmart Canada, spent more than 30 years learning this the hard way. At one point, just hours before a flight, he cancelled a major conference trip rather than pushing through. He explained it perfectly: “I need to slow things down to go fast.” If rest restores you, then you’re tired, and that’s normal. If it doesn’t, that’s your signal to stop, act, and talk to a medical professional.

3. Trace your wiring.

Chester Elton is known worldwide as the Apostle of Appreciation. So when he told me that for the first part of his career he was “an absolute jerk,” I almost fell out of my chair.

Chester had what he calls a magical childhood—a big, loving family filled with faith and service. But he was the youngest of five boys, and if you didn’t eat fast, you didn’t eat. You worked hard, you competed, and you won. That followed him to school and into his career, and it paid off. Bigger house, great vacations, and the corner office. What he couldn’t see was who he was becoming. His wife Heidi would catch him yelling in the shower, replaying work conversations. Then one evening on a walk around the neighborhood, she said, “I don’t care what we do, but we are not doing this anymore. I want my husband back. This is not who you are.”

Even a happy childhood can teach you that effort is how good people prove they’re good, and that worth is something you earn. For a lot of us, the wiring goes back generations. Marj Rehman, founder of Envoi, comes from four generations of immigrants: India to Pakistan to Dubai to Canada. He told me there has always been an urgency in life, a feeling that there is no rest. As a child of immigrants myself, I know that feeling in my bones.

This is where the burnout loop starts. The wiring is set in childhood. Then a culture that celebrates overwork rewards it. Over time, a sacrifice starts to feel like obligation—until something forces you to stop. Ask yourself: who taught me what success looks like? And did anyone ever tell me when to stop?

4. Refuse to be a stump.

Years ago, I was driving home on a 10-lane highway in Houston, Texas, after a brutal day at work, and suddenly I couldn’t breathe. My chest was tight. I was dizzy. My whole body was shutting down. I pulled over and called 911 because I thought I was having a heart attack. The hospital discharged me, and the next morning I went back to work like nothing had happened. This is what I call the sacrifice myth in action. It’s the belief that if you want to be successful, it’s supposed to hurt.

“Over time, a sacrifice starts to feel like obligation—until something forces you to stop.”

You may have grown up with The Giving Tree. It’s a book about a boy and a tree, and the tree loves the boy. As the boy grows up, he takes her apples to sell, her branches to build a house, and her trunk to build a boat. At the end, there’s nothing left of her but a stump—and we’re told she’s happy. As a child, I thought it was a beautiful story of love. Now, as an adult, it makes me want to scream. It teaches us that love and loyalty are proven by disappearing. My teenager and I have a saying. When she sees me self-sacrifice, she puts her arm on my shoulder and she says, “Mom, don’t be a stump.”

We do this with work all the time. We give pain and sacrifice a purpose, and that’s supposed to make it better. We treat the suffering itself as proof that we’re serious, committed, and worthy. But work is an exchange. You give it your skill, your time, and your commitment. In return, you get a livelihood, growth, recognition, agency, and impact. When the price is your health, relationships, or humanity, it’s no longer an exchange. That is self-abandonment. That’s becoming a stump.

The opposite of martyrdom isn’t quiet quitting or bed rotting. It’s stewardship—taking care of your energy, knowing your limits, and building a life you can actually sustain.

5. Be more than your title.

Stacy Brown-Philpot spent nearly two decades climbing from Google to CEO of TaskRabbit, where she led the company through its acquisition by IKEA. When she stepped down, it was the first time in almost twenty years she didn’t have a title. She found herself asking, “If I’m not a CEO, then who am I?”

The offers kept coming—a public company, a private company, each one exactly what she was “supposed” to do next. People told her, “We don’t have enough Black women CEOs. You need to get back in there.”

That’s the identity myth: the idea that what I do is who I am. What makes it so insidious is that we’re rewarded for it. If you start disappearing into a romantic relationship, someone who loves you will pull you aside; if you disappear into your work, you’ll get applauded.

“What makes it so insidious is that we’re rewarded for it.”

Every job has an end, whether that means a layoff or retirement. If your whole self lives in one role, losing that role feels like losing yourself. Think of it like a house: work isn’t the foundation. It’s an important room that, during some seasons, you’ll spend a lot of time in. But you can’t board up every other room for 20 years.

I once opened a session for senior leaders with a simple question: “Tell me who you are without telling me what you do.” Long pauses. Nervous laughter. Most of them had never reflected on that question. So try it. You might be someone’s steady presence, the friend who remembers birthdays, the neighbor who shovels the snow, or the person in your family who makes a mean stack of pancakes. Those aren’t small things. Those are the joys that life is built on.

Stop pretending you’re fine. Stop pretending your life can wait until the next milestone.

#10347. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.

Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.

There are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.

Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.

I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.

So, with that said, let’s focus on the fundamentals.

Google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen shows options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”

Those new features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.

One of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.

UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.

On that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.

The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.

Rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.

I really just wish it would have a rechargeable battery, preferably via USB-C. It would have been the only tracker on the market to support UWB and be rechargeable.

I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!

Google Pixel Tag is now available at the Google Store and Amazon.

#10346. Friday the 13th is here. Its impact on your work day may not be so scary

Business can be risky, so it’s natural that superstitions can sometimes creep in when money and careers are at stake.

This workweek ends on Friday the 13th, so in the Western world, the stage is set for fear to influence commerce.

Let’s take a look at the so-called bad luck day’s origins and how it impacts the business world.

What is a fear of Friday the 13th called?

A fear of Friday the 13th is called “paraskevidekatriaphobia,” a term created by psychotherapist Donald Dossey. It combines the Greek words for Friday, 13, and fear.

How many Friday the 13ths are there in a year?

Around every 212.35 days, a Friday the 13th occurs. This figure is based on a complete 400-year Gregorian calendar cycle.

Another way to look at it: there is at least one Friday the 13th a year, but there can be up to three. This year, 2026, Friday the 13th will be in triplicate.

When did Friday the 13th become unlucky?

The truth is, no one really knows how exactly Friday the 13th became synonymous with misfortune.

There are historical and religious references that might shed some light. One of the theories is that the number 12 is considered perfect and complete, so by comparison, 13 is less than.

A popular retelling of Norse mythology states that 12 gods were having a banquet in Valhalla until Loki showed up uninvited, bringing their numbers to 13. The unwelcome guest was able to trick the blind god Höd into killing his brother Balder.

The number 13 and the day Friday also show up in Christianity. According to Christian teachings, there were 13 people present at the Last Supper, which occurred on a Thursday.

The following day, Jesus was crucified. Many also believe Eve gave Adam the forbidden fruit from the tree of knowledge and Cain killed Abel on a Friday.

Where does Friday the 13th show up in pop culture?

History does have examples of traumatic events happening on Friday the 13th. One of these occurred in 1307 when King Philip IV of France detained numerous members of the Knights Templar. Some of these men were eventually executed.

Friday the 13th also shows up in literature. In 1834, an article in Revue de Paris by Marquis de Salvo, entitled “Le Chateau de Carini,” told the story of a filicide committed by a Sicilian count on Friday the 13th.

In 1907, American author Thomas William Lawson published the novel Friday, the Thirteenth, about a stockbroker who crashes the market on the title date.

Perhaps the best modern example of Friday the 13th mania is Sean S. Cunningham’s slasher film franchise, which began in 1980. Jason Voorhees’s hockey goalie mask has become iconic.

Crystal Lake, a prequel series produced by A24, is the latest from the franchise and currently streaming on Peacock.

How does superstition impact business?

In 2006, the same Dr. Dossey, who named the fear of Friday the 13th, also claimed Americans lost $800 to $900 million due to lost productivity driven by fear of the day. However, his nontransparent methodology to get to those figures has drawn criticism. The Wall Street Journal is just one of the publications that questioned its validity.

Although it’s hard to quantify an exact figure, the impact of the fear of Friday the 13th can be found.

In Manhattan and Brooklyn, less than 5% of mid-rise and high-rise residential condo buildings have a floor labeled 13, WSJ reports.

According to Realting.com, 13th-floor apartments are purchased 18% less often on average than their counterparts located on other floors. Apartment sales are also down on the day itself, 19% on any given 13th.

Ironically, a 2007 USA Today/Gallup poll found that only 13% of Americans would be bothered if required to stay on the 13th floor of a hotel. A spooky statistic indeed.

#10345. One-Shot Any Web App with Gradio's gr.HTML

Gradio 6 quietly shipped a very powerful feature: gr.HTML now supports custom templates, scoped CSS, and JavaScript interactivity. Which means you can build pretty much any web component — and Claude (or any other frontier LLM) can generate the whole thing in one shot: frontend, backend, and state management, all in a single Python file.

We tested this by building different types of apps. Each one is a single Python file, no build step, deployable to Hugging Face Spaces in seconds.

Pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

The tree animation alone would normally require a separate React component. Here it's just CSS keyframes in css_template and state updates in js_on_load.

GitHub Contribution Heatmap: Click any cell to toggle contributions. Multiple color themes. Pattern generators (streaks, seasonal, random). Live stats that update as you edit.

Kanban Board: Full drag-and-drop between columns. Inline editing (double-click any card). Search feature that can filter in real-time. Collapsible columns.

Drag-and-drop usually means pulling in a library. Here it's native HTML5 drag events wired up in js_on_load, with state synced back to Python via trigger('change').

Spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The community's built some creative components with gr.HTML too:

3D Camera Control for Image Editing: A full Three.js viewport inside a Gradio app! Drag handles to control azimuth, elevation, and distance. Your uploaded image appears in the 3D scene, and the camera parameters feed directly into Qwen's latest image editing model. These kinds of interactive 3D controls would normally require a separate frontend — with Gradio it's just one gr.HTML subclass🔥

Real-time Speech Transcription: Live transcription with Mistral's Voxtral model. The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

Every gr.HTML component takes three templates:

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

For reusable components, subclass gr.HTML:

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

When you ask your LLM to build a custom component, single-file output is everything. No "now create the styles file" or "wire this into your build config." Just one Python file that runs immediately.

The feedback loop becomes: describe what you want → get code → gradio app.py → see it working → describe what to fix → repeat. Each cycle takes seconds with Gradio's reload mode.

Deploy to Spaces with gradio deploy or share a temporary link with demo.launch(share=True). Within a few seconds from an idea to a live app.

Gradio ships with 32 interactive components, but sometimes your perfect AI web app needs something special. That's where gr.HTML comes in.

If you’ve got an idea, try building it with gr.HTML: describe what you want to your LLM, generate the code, run it. You might be surprised what you can ship in 5 minutes.

#10343. How to survive the loss of an irreplaceable leader

The challenge of replacing Jensen Huang, the visionary co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, who resigned yesterday morning amid reports of extramarital affairs, may be daunting—but it is far from unprecedented.

While research shows that companies moving on from a founding CEO face a higher risk of failure or downturn than other CEO transitions, major corporations from Apple to Amazon have successfully managed the loss of a larger-than-life presence at the top of the corporate ladder.

Management experts who have studied such transitions say there are a few key lessons.

Don’t look for a carbon copy of the founder

When Tim Cook replaced legendary Apple founder Steve Jobs in 2011, speculation suggested he might try to replicate Jobs’ style, right down to the signature turtleneck and jeans. However, experts warned against directly replicating Jobs’ leadership and management style.

 “A copy of anyone is going to come off looking bad,” Wharton management professor Peter Cappelli said. “It will never be as good as the original, and people will spend their time focusing on the differences.”

Cook succeeded by building on Apple’s strengths and emphasizing his expertise as an operations specialist, scaling the sophisticated global supply chain he helped build as chief operating officer to increase annual revenue nearly fourfold.

Instead of positioning himself as a visionary like his legendary predecessor, Cook maintained an understated management style and let the company’s massive financial success speak for itself. Cook says he urged his own successor, John Ternus, to take his own individual approach.

“Don’t mimic me, just like I didn’t mimic Steve,” Cook recalled telling Ternus in a recent interview with The Independent. “We all have different strengths.”

Give the successor real authority—and make sure the founder lets go

While research shows transitions are more successful when founders feel involved in the planning process, once they step down, it is important they keep their distance.

“The presence of two prominent leaders can confuse the organization and hinder the success of the successor CEO,” executive search firm Spencer Stuart wrote in 2024. “There can only be one CEO.”

The firm recommends having explicit conversations among the founder, successor, and the board to clearly distinguish the founder’s responsibilities from those of the new chief executive.

Spencer Stuart also examined 200 U.S. companies with executive chairmen (leaders, often former or founding executives, who preside over the board of directors while also remaining involved in daily business operations and management) and found that 54% underperformed their peers during the executive chair’s tenure—by an average of 14%.

Give the corporate culture room to breathe

Often, successful founders dictate not only their company’s strategy but also its internal culture. Workplace norms, management practices, and the company’s identity become a reflection of their personal style and values. While employees can become deeply attached to those traditions, that doesn’t mean they will work for the founder’s successor.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has spoken frequently about how he adjusted the company’s culture after taking over from Bill Gates’ successor, Steve Ballmer, in 2014.

Sensing that the company needed to rethink its hard-charging internal culture, Nadella sought to reduce internal division and promote collaboration: in his words, move from a “know-it-all” mindset to a “learn-it-all” one. One of his policies was to ensure individual performance reviews reflected how employees contributed to others’ success.

“Achieving our mission requires us to evolve our culture,” Nadella says. “It all starts with a growth mindset—a passion to learn and bring our best every day to make a bigger difference in the world.”

The changes accompanied a broader strategic transformation that helped Microsoft become a leader in cloud computing and AI. Annual revenue has more than tripled, from $87 billion in 2014 to $282 billion in 2025.

Start by planning ahead

Unfortunately for Nvidia, it appears the company has not engaged in what many experts consider one of the most important aspects of a smooth transition: planning ahead. The best chief executives work with their directors on succession planning throughout their tenure to ensure the company is protected in an emergency.

According to McKinsey, former Intuit CEO Brad Smith gave the board a quarterly verbal update on his succession plan and held an official succession planning session once a year. During the session, company leaders would consider potential candidates and adjust their criteria for the next CEO to adapt to the market.

Experts also say the best transitions often have a firm timeline.  

“Without a clear timetable, grooming internal successors and following an orderly succession process become challenging,” former Medtronic CEO and Harvard Business School professor Bill George has said.  

For Nvidia, the preparation may have to happen in reverse. Huang spent more than three decades building a company around his technical vision, unconventional management style, and personal authority. His successor will now have to determine which parts of that legacy are essential to Nvidia’s success—and which can be jettisoned.

In fact, this transition might be the final test of Huang’s leadership. In the words of management expert Jim Collins: “If your company cannot be great without you, it is not yet a great company.”

#10342. Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters

No one loves ads, but generally people will tolerate them if it means getting something free or at a lower price. What people won’t forgive? Being lied to.

A study looking at how consumers see native ads on news sites—which look similar to editorial content, just with labels—found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising. And when people find out after the fact, they don’t take it well. In a Contently survey, two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand.

That’s why there’s a whole set of regulations and standards around advertising disclosures that are meant to protect consumers. Now that AI is slowly becoming a central part of our media ecosystem, it’s unclear to what extent those disclosures should carry over into AI answers. After all, if the public is increasingly using AI to shop (47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, according to an impact.com survey, and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse), it feels intuitive that the user should see plainly the commercial interests of the sites that informed any answer.

Truth in labeling?

A reliable label in AI sounds like a good idea, but it gets complicated quickly. For starters, the label might cause confusion that the AI platform itself was paid rather than the original publisher. In the case of ChatGPT that would potentially conflict with its own ads, which are separate from the answer and labeled as sponsored. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure question, so far, is the citation link: since launching ChatGPT search, it has included links to sources in answers so users can check them for themselves.

All of this gets at the fundamental question of judgment, and which parts of judging a source users have handed over to AI, consciously or unconsciously, simply by using it. When you ask AI to come up with, say, recommendations for air fryers, it’s more like hiring a researcher, not looking at a billboard. In fact, some people turn to AI precisely to get away from the billboards: 24% of the shoppers in the impact.com survey said they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads. You trust it to hoover up all the information it can find about the question, weigh all the factors—including whether or not any sources are sponsored—and give you the best possible answer.

How important is a label at that point? It’d be silly to ask a researcher to stamp every brochure they look at, and pass those brochures over to you in a pile. If AI can solve some of humanity’s most intractable math problems, it can probably reliably weigh the commercial intent of a brand’s FAQ page. In fact, you could argue a label in the answer might cause the reader to overscrutinize an answer the AI has already deemed the most useful possible.

AI’s affiliate addiction

If we’re considering disclosures, we need to talk about affiliate content, and AI’s outsize reliance on it. As you might imagine, for any query about buying decisions, AI seeks out product recommendations. Those articles are often supported by affiliate revenue, meaning the site gets a fee when the reader takes action, typically a purchase. Legitimate sites that monetize via affiliate disclose that fact on any page with affiliate links; indeed, FTC guidelines require that they do so.

However, almost none of those disclosures survive the journey into an AI answer. AI summaries rely heavily on affiliate content: one study found that about a quarter of the pages cited by ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews, and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure, and 86% of answers cited at least one such page. If those disclosures carried over, they’d be in almost every shopping answer. Beyond the UI nightmare that would result, would the label have any meaning at that point?

To be clear, no one’s arguing that disclosures don’t matter generally. Journalists take them very seriously, and they should. The SPJ code says to “distinguish news from advertising and shun hybrids that blur the lines.” Recommendation sites like Wirecutter or The Strategist make their business model clear, on every page, to everyone who cares to know.

The number of people who care to know, however, is likely rather low. When Pew tracked how people actually use Google, they clicked a link inside an AI summary on just 1% of visits. According to impact.com’s survey, Gen Z is split between those who never click through (11%) and those who always do (21%). That doesn’t contradict the anger over native ads: People hate finding out they were misled, but that’s different from wanting to audit every source up front. Again, auditing the sources is exactly the job they’re handing to the AI. While it wouldn’t solve all issues, you can picture a world where AI users have the option of seeing labels or not, perhaps via something like a “flag paid sources” toggle.

The kickback question

The label debate, however, misses the real concern. Anyone familiar with today’s models understands that AI can tell the difference between paid content and editorial (being able to tell isn’t the same as being impossible to game, but that’s another column). What is less clear are the commercial interests of the platform itself. In the researcher analogy, you might trust the judgment of the person you hired—that’s why you hired them. But you also want to be assured they’re not getting kickbacks from anyone they’re recommending. That worry isn’t hypothetical. In a University of Michigan study, people rarely noticed when a chatbot wove ads into its responses, and many actually preferred those answers. Even when the ads were labeled, about half the participants didn’t spot them.

This concern is at the heart of OpenAI’s promise that “ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you,” which is directly from its ad principles. Ads only appear in ChatGPT’s free and Go tiers, and they always appear separate from the answer itself. Perplexity made similar promises when advertising was part of its business model, though it walked away from ads earlier this year, with one executive saying, “A user needs to believe this is the best possible answer.”

OpenAI’s promise is important because of the trust factor, which is evident when you look at conversion rates. Conversion from OpenAI ads is considerably lower than from the answers themselves. Early research from the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management found shoppers who clicked ChatGPT ads bought at a rate of 0.37%, versus 2.21% for those who arrived through ChatGPT’s regular answers. 

That makes sense—the answer gives what the model deems the “right” recommendation whereas an ad is just one of those options trying to sell you something. It also explains why OpenAI has every reason to keep that wall up. The moment answers look bought, they’ll convert like ads. Logically, this incentivizes brands to prioritize presence in AI answers over advertising. Not only are you more likely to drive business, you can also reach the people who pay for ChatGPT, who never see ads at all (and thus are more likely to pay for other things, like your product).

As I found out in my tests with Meta’s Muse, it will generally recommend what you can actually buy within Muse. When I asked it which robot vacuum was the best for me, it recommended a model that I could check out right there, but was not the top model on the review it cited. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said directly that Muse would monetize via transactions. On Meta’s October earnings call, he said the company will “build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate.” That suggests Muse will have every reason to consider what’s best for Meta when it steers you toward product decisions.

An agent you can trust

Concerns over agent influence have sparked calls for engineering “loyalty by design” in agentic systems, a phrase from Consumer Reports’ work on AI agents. The idea: agents should always put the needs and desires of the user first, and make transparent any other considerations, or even conflicts, they might have when finding information or carrying out actions. Sen. Mark Warner has floated draft legislation that would write a similar duty of loyalty into law for some AI agents.

There’s a strong case to be made that the market will correct for this: If any particular agent doesn’t act in the user’s interest in a material way, there’s certainly plenty of competition. That assumes switching is easy, though. An agent that knows your email, your calendar and what you bought last month is a lot harder to fire than a search engine.

Ultimately the fight over commercial labels is a good instinct, but it aims the question of trust at the wrong target. By using AI, I’m implicitly trusting the agent’s judgment to find the best information to answer my query. The better question is whether the agent is loyal, and how I can check. Labels protect readers from sketchy sources. What protects us from sketchy agents hasn’t been invented yet.

#10341. Top 6 AI YouTube Transcript Generators: Features, Accuracy, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

There is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Is it legal to transcribe someone else's YouTube video? Transcribing for personal research or accessibility is common, but republishing the text may infringe copyright. Check the video's license and YouTube's terms, and get permission when in doubt.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

The Made by Google 2026 lineup is finally complete with tomorrow’s retail launch of the Pixel Tag. You can find our review here, while there are some additional details about the device since the August announcement.

The Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker with NFC. Google did not mention this connectivity specification in August, with Near Field Communication letting you tap the tracker to the back of your phone to immediately open device settings. The NFC area on the Pixel Tag is below the circular battery door, which you hold down and twist counterclockwise to open.

On Android 17 QPR2, tapping immediately opens the details page. On QPR1, you first get a system notification that you need to click. NFC joins Bluetooth 6.0 with Channel Sounding and Ultra Wideband (UWB).
